summary: Dominik Kundel leads a 16-person Emerging Tech & Innovation team at Twilio, operating outside the company's two main business units (Communications API and Customer Data Platform). The team explores disruptive innovation in customer engagement while Twilio treats AI as a feature across all products. Kundel frames the work through the Innovator's Dilemma: sustaining innovation iterates on existing products for known customers, while disruptive innovation targets niches with initially lower quality. AI is unique because both types advance rapidly—non-threats can become threats overnight, as ChatGPT's impact on Google Search showed. Agents and GPTs aren't enterprise-ready due to quality, cost, and regulatory barriers; enterprises see AI as cost-saving while agents remain expensive, but startups and SMBs see agents as value-additive. The team began as a 3-person Skunk Works group prototyping a customer engagement flywheel between Twilio's CDP and Communications platform, building an AI Personalization Engine (RAG on Segment profiles) and AI Perception Engine (extracting conversation insights)—together forming a customer memory concept. Handing these to R&D failed because the work was disruptive, solving niche use cases without market momentum against R&D's profitability focus. Learning from this, the team shifted to hackathons, dogfooding via an IT help desk, and building AI Assistant, an agent builder on customer memory. A new challenge emerged as GenAI inverts the traditional product development lifecycle: prototypes and MVPs can be built rapidly without prior data, but shipping below the normal quality bar risks customer trust. To solve this, Twilio studied GitNext (GitHub Copilot) and Cloudflare Emerging Technologies, both focused on setting appropriate expectations around reliability, capabilities, and availability. They created the Twilio Alpha sub-brand to ship early and often, open waitlists for developer previews, and onboard customers quickly. For speed, they hired for curiosity and creativity over existing AI experience, assumed every model would be redundant tomorrow (evaluating new models like 3.5 Sonnet within a day), and maintained roadmap flexibility by distinguishing stable expectations (trust and safety) from shifting ones (multimodality trends). A final mistake was over-isolation in year one—operating on a need-to-know basis so internal teams didn't know the team existed. This produced the third learning: share as you go, both internally to find collaboration opportunities and externally to help B2B customers be thought leaders. These three learnings became the team's base principles: customer and developer obsession, shipping early and often, building a curious problem-owning team, and sharing as they go.

sections.title: Introduction and Team Overview
sections.summary: Kundel introduces himself and the Emerging Tech & Innovation team at Twilio—16 people across engineering, product, design, and go-to-market. The team operates outside Twilio's two main business units (Communications API and Customer Data Platform) and explores the future of customer engagement with emerging technologies. AI is treated as a feature across all products, not a separate team function.

sections.title: Sustaining vs Disruptive Innovation in AI
sections.summary: Kundel distinguishes sustaining innovation (iterative improvements for existing customers) from disruptive innovation (initially lower quality, niche-focused). AI advances both types simultaneously. Agents and GPTs are disruptive but not enterprise-ready due to quality, cost, and regulatory issues. Enterprises see AI as cost-saving while agents are expensive; startups and SMBs see agents as value-additive. The rapid daily quality shifts in AI make ignoring disruptive innovation dangerous, as demonstrated by ChatGPT's impact on Google Search.

sections.title: Team Origins and First AI Projects
sections.summary: The team started as a 3-person Skunk Works group prototyping a customer engagement flywheel between Twilio's CDP and Communications platform. LLMs were a natural fit for bridging unstructured communications and structured customer data. They built two systems: the AI Personalization Engine (RAG on Segment customer profiles) and the AI Perception Engine (extracting customer insights from conversations), together forming a customer memory concept.

sections.title: Challenges and Evolved Approach
sections.summary: The first handoff to R&D failed because the work was disruptive innovation solving a niche use case without enough market momentum against profitability-focused sustaining innovation. The team then built AI Assistant, an agent builder on customer memory, and changed tactics: running internal hackathons with rough prototypes, dogfooding via IT help desk, and establishing engineering foundations. A new challenge emerged as GenAI inverts the traditional product development lifecycle, creating tension with Twilio's established trust-building processes.

sections.title: Shipping Early, Moving Fast, and Sharing Openly
sections.summary: GenAI enables rapid prototyping without prior data, but shipping below normal quality bars risks customer trust. Studying GitNext and Cloudflare Emerging Technologies, Twilio created the Twilio Alpha sub-brand to set appropriate expectations and ship early and often via developer preview waitlists. For speed, they hired for curiosity and creativity over existing AI experience, assumed every model would be redundant tomorrow (evaluating new models like 3.5 Sonnet within a day), and maintained roadmap flexibility by distinguishing stable expectations (trust and safety) from shifting ones (multimodality). A final mistake was over-isolation in year one, sharing work only on a need-to-know basis so internal teams didn't know they existed. This produced the third learning: share as you go, internally for collaboration and externally to help B2B customers be thought leaders. All three learnings became the team's base principles: customer/developer obsession, shipping early and often, building a curious problem-owning team, and sharing as they go.
